questions.question: What problem does the Paxos algorithm solve?

options.text: Achieving consensus among distributed nodes even with failures

questions.explanation: Paxos solves distributed consensus: getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed/lost. Fundamental for replicated state machines.

questions.question: What are the three roles in basic Paxos?
questions.explanation: Proposer: proposes values. Acceptor: votes on proposals, forms quorums. Learner: learns the chosen value. In practice, a single node often plays multiple roles.

questions.question: What are the two phases of basic Paxos?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (Prepare): Proposer sends prepare(n), acceptors promise not to accept lower proposals. Phase 2 (Accept): If majority promised, proposer sends accept(n, value), acceptors accept if they haven't promised higher.

questions.question: What is a quorum in Paxos?

options.text: A majority of acceptors (more than half)

questions.explanation: Quorum = majority of acceptors. With 5 acceptors, quorum is 3. Any two quorums overlap by at least one node, ensuring consistency. This allows progress even with minority failures.

questions.question: Why does Paxos use proposal numbers?

options.text: To order proposals and ensure only the highest-numbered proposal can succeed

questions.explanation: Proposal numbers (n) create ordering. Acceptors promise to reject proposals with lower numbers. If a proposer's prepare is rejected, it retries with a higher number. Prevents conflicts between concurrent proposers.

questions.question: What happens if an acceptor receives a prepare request with a number lower than one it already promised?
questions.explanation: Acceptors track the highest proposal number they've promised. If prepare(n) arrives where n < promised, they reject it. The proposer must retry with a higher number.

questions.question: What is Multi-Paxos?

options.text: An optimization where a stable leader skips Phase 1 for subsequent consensus rounds

questions.explanation: Basic Paxos decides one value. Multi-Paxos: elect a leader who can skip Phase 1 for subsequent values (already has promises). Much more efficient for replicated logs. Most practical implementations use Multi-Paxos.

questions.question: What is a key challenge with implementing Paxos?

options.text: The algorithm is notoriously difficult to understand and implement correctly
It only works with two nodes

questions.explanation: Paxos is famously hard to understand (even Lamport rewrote his paper). Edge cases, liveness issues, and the gap between theory and implementation make it error-prone. This led to Raft's creation.

questions.question: Can Paxos make progress if a majority of nodes fail?

options.text: Yes, it can always make progress
No, it requires a majority (quorum) of acceptors to be available

questions.explanation: Paxos requires quorum (majority) for both phases. With 5 nodes, if 3 fail, no quorum can form. The system blocks until enough nodes recover. This is the tradeoff for consistency.

questions.question: What does Paxos guarantee about the chosen value?

options.text: The value will be the first one proposed
Once a value is chosen, all future rounds will choose the same value (safety)
All nodes will have the value immediately

questions.explanation: Paxos safety: once a value is chosen (accepted by quorum), it's permanent. Any future successful proposal will propose the same value. This is achieved through the prepare phase learning previously accepted values.

questions.question: Which systems use Paxos or Paxos-like algorithms?
questions.explanation: Chubby uses Paxos. ZooKeeper uses ZAB (Paxos-like). DynamoDB uses Paxos for metadata coordination. MySQL's default replication is async, not consensus-based (though Group Replication uses Paxos).

questions.question: What is the 'dueling proposers' problem in Paxos?

options.text: Two proposers continuously preempting each other with higher proposal numbers, preventing progress

questions.explanation: Livelock scenario: Proposer A prepares(1), Proposer B prepares(2) preempts, A prepares(3) preempts, B prepares(4)... No progress. Solutions: random backoff, leader election, or Multi-Paxos with stable leader.
